questions.question: Which opening move wins this fight most cleanly?

moves.name: Integration by Parts with u = x^2, dv = sin x dx
moves.professor: Polynomial times trig: set polynomial as u and fire IBP. Two rounds and the enemy falls.

moves.name: Tabular Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Tabular is just IBP in disciplined formation. Works perfectly here.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = sin x)
moves.professor: Nowhere to go with that du. You've just handed the enemy an opening.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No root of a quadratic means no trig sub. You're reading the battlefield wrong.

questions.question: Choose the most lethal first strike.

moves.name: Integration by Parts with u = ln x, dv = 1/x^2 dx
moves.professor: ln x must be u; its derivative simplifies the fight. IBP dispatches it in one blow.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = ln x)
moves.professor: That leaves ∫ u/e^u du, which is worse. You've walked into a trap.

moves.name: Recognize as derivative of -(ln x + 1)/x
moves.professor: Sharp eye, but relying on memorized forms is risky in the heat of battle. IBP is the reliable blade.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: ln x is not a rational function. You're swinging at a ghost.

questions.question: What strategy breaks this open?

moves.name: Save a cos x, convert cos^2 x to 1 - sin^2 x, then u = sin x
moves.professor: Odd power of cosine gifts you du. The rest turns into a simple polynomial in sin x. Clean kill.

moves.name: Use power-reduction formulas for both sin^2 x and cos^3 x
moves.professor: A grind, but it will get you there. Much slower, though—burning unnecessary time.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No square root, no quadratic. Wrong weapon entirely.

moves.name: Integration by Parts with u = sin^2 x, dv = cos^3 x dx
moves.professor: IBP with pure trig powers leads nowhere except into a thorn bush.

questions.question: Which approach delivers a swift victory?

moves.name: Complete the square to ((x+1)^2 + 1), then arctan
moves.professor: An irreducible quadratic hides an arctan. Complete the square and the path is clear.

moves.name: Partial Fractions using complex roots
moves.professor: Wading into the complex plane when a simple arctan awaits is a tactical detour, not a shortcut.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 + 2x + 2)
moves.professor: du = 2x+2, not a constant. The strike misses completely.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: No product to separate. IBP has no anchor here.

questions.question: Identify the most elegant finish for this integral.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 + 3x - 10)
moves.professor: The numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator. One substitution, one logarithm. Done.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: You can factor and decompose, but it's like using a siege engine on a single soldier. Too slow.

moves.name: Complete the square and use trigonometric substitution
moves.professor: A needless detour through trig when a clean u-sub is staring at you. Stay focused.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Rational functions not in product form don't yield to IBP. You'll just stumble.

questions.question: What is the surest tactical move here?

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = 4 - x^2)
moves.professor: The x in the numerator is the perfect partner for du. One simple change of variable ends it.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = 2 sin θ)
moves.professor: This route is safe but leaves you with extra trig simplification. Valid, but not optimal.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: No product form. IBP has no grip on a radical denominator.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: The square root blocks any decomposition. That wall won't crack.

questions.question: Choose the method that cuts deepest.

moves.name: Integration by Parts twice and solve for the integral
moves.professor: The classic loop. IBP brings the same integral back, allowing you to isolate it. A flawless tactical loop.

moves.name: Use Euler's formula to rewrite sin x
moves.professor: Turning the fight into complex exponentials also wins. Slightly advanced, but elegant.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = sin x)
moves.professor: e^x doesn't pair well with that substitution. You'll get tangled in recursive mess.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No square root of a quadratic. Wrong battle, wrong weapon.

questions.question: What is the critical first step to evaluate this?

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = tan x)
moves.professor: sec^2 x dx is exactly du. The integral reduces to ∫ u^3 du. A single, decisive blow.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = sec x)
moves.professor: That would leave you with ∫ (u^2-1) u du, which works, but why take the longer path to the same kill?

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: No need for IBP when the substitution is this clean. Overthinking on the battlefield gets you hit.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: Trig sub is for radicals, not pure powers of trig functions. Misfire.

questions.question: Which weapon is most appropriate here?

moves.name: Rewrite as (x-2)^{-2} and use power rule
moves.professor: The denominator is a perfect square. No need for fancy tactics; just a simple power rule.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Indeed it factors into (x-2)^2, but the decomposition just gives back the same form. A wasted swing.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No root means trig sub is dead on arrival. Keep your eyes on the target.

moves.name: Complete the square then arctan formula
moves.professor: Completing the square reveals (x-2)^2, leading to a power, not an arctan. You'd realize your mistake, but time is burned.

questions.question: Pick the most lethal approach.

moves.name: Product-to-Sum Identity
moves.professor: Mix of sine and cosine with different frequencies screams product-to-sum. Two easy integrals remain.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP will cycle you around these products endlessly. A trap—step back.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = sin(5x) or cos(2x))
moves.professor: Derivatives don't align. You'll be left with a mismatch and a mess.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical. Wrong war.

questions.question: Which move dominates this encounter?

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = 3 sec θ)
moves.professor: √(x^2 - a^2) is the banner of secant substitution. The radical turns into tan θ and the fight simplifies.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 - 9)
moves.professor: You'll end up with a mismatched power of u that leaves an x alive. Ambush.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: The radical blocks any rational decomposition. You can't breach that.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Radical with x in denominator doesn't yield to IBP. Your weapon just slides off.

questions.question: What is the sharpest opening strike?

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = 1 - x^2)
moves.professor: An odd power of x outside the root and x^2 inside? u-sub turns it into a simple polynomial fight.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = sin θ)
moves.professor: That works and is the standard path, but the u-sub is faster here. You still get the kill.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP with a fractional power radical? You'll sink into a quagmire.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Not a rational function; partial fractions have no power here.

questions.question: Identify the path of least resistance.

moves.name: Split into ∫ x/(x^2+1) dx + ∫ 1/(x^2+1) dx
moves.professor: One integral is a simple ln substitution, the other an arctan. Divide and conquer—two clean strikes.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (x = tan θ)
moves.professor: This route works on the whole thing, but you'll do extra work for no gain. Still a win.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Denominator is irreducible. Partial fractions cannot strike this target.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Not a product; IBP is useless here.

questions.question: What is the killing blow for this integral?

moves.name: Integration by Parts with u = sec x, dv = sec^2 x dx
moves.professor: The classic. IBP creates an equation involving ∫ sec^3 x, which you then isolate. Surgical strike.

moves.name: Rewrite as ∫ (1 + tan^2 x) sec x dx, then substitution
moves.professor: This path becomes messy, leading to an integral of sec x with extra steps. Not a killing blow, just a skirmish.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical inside an integral of a pure trig function. You're lost on the battlefield.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Not rational. That weapon can't even dent this target.

questions.question: Which strategy guarantees a quick win?

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^3)
moves.professor: The derivative of the exponent is 3x^2, sitting right there. One substitution and the enemy evaporates.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP against a non-linear exponent will wrap you in loops. A fatal misstep.

moves.name: Tabular Integration by Parts
moves.professor: Tabular needs a linear argument inside the exponential. Here it shatters on impact.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: Not a quadratic root. Weapon mismatch.

questions.question: Choose the most efficient opening move.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution (2x = 3 tan θ)
moves.professor: The form √(u^2 + a^2) calls for tangent. The whole integral simplifies to a manageable trig term.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = 4x^2 + 9)
moves.professor: You'll have an extra x that won't vanish. The blade catches in the armor.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: The square root blocks all rational attempts. This wall won't break.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: IBP doesn't know what to do with a radical in the denominator. Pointless swing.

questions.question: Which method cuts through the clutter?

moves.name: Use power-reduction formulas (cos^2 x = (1+cos 2x)/2) twice
moves.professor: Even power of cosine: lower the exponent until you get linear trig functions. Systematic defeat.

moves.name: Rewrite as (cos^2 x)^2 and use integration by parts
moves.professor: IBP on pure powers of trig leads to infinite loops with no exit. You'll exhaust yourself.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = cos x)
moves.professor: Where's the sin x to give du? Missing in action.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical. You're bringing the wrong playbook.

questions.question: Quickly, what is the best tactic?

moves.name: Integration by Parts with u = arctan x, dv = x dx
moves.professor: An inverse trig multiplied by a polynomial: let the inverse be u. IBP delivers a clean rational remainder.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = arctan x)
moves.professor: That leaves you with ∫ u (tan u) sec^2 u du, a far worse monster. You've fed the enemy.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No root. Off-target.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: arctan x is not rational. This blade shatters.

questions.question: What is the critical move?

moves.name: Complete the square, then use arctan formula
moves.professor: Denominator is (x-3)^2 + 4. An arctan awaits. Straight to victory.

moves.name: Partial Fractions
moves.professor: Irreducible quadratic over reals. You can't break it further. Your weapon bounces off.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = x^2 - 6x + 13)
moves.professor: du = 2x-6, no constant numerator. Strike fails.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: No product. IBP is a ghost here.

questions.question: Spot the trap and choose the true path.

moves.name: Use sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, split into ∫ csc x /2 dx + ∫ sec x /2 dx
moves.professor: Double-angle identity clears the disguise. Then two standard integrals end the duel.

moves.name: u-Substitution (u = sin 2x)
moves.professor: The numerator doesn't align with du. You'll stagger into a dead end.

moves.name: Integration by Parts
moves.professor: No product of different function types. IBP has no foothold.

moves.name: Trigonometric Substitution
moves.professor: No radical. You've misidentified the enemy.
